First listed 2026-05-27 · episode or wrap

Inside the Hidden Consumer Crisis with Lakshmi Ganapathi

Lakshmi Ganapathi argues that inflation, BNPL dependence and opaque credit structures reveal strain hidden by benign bank statistics. She connects these concerns to shorts in FICO, Wingstop, AutoZone, Group 1 and DoorDash. Eisman challenges the missing bank-loss evidence, adopts selected Wingstop and refinancing explanations, and distinguishes near-term noise from future software-loan maturities. Inflation and several BNPL figures are supported, while claims about universal borrower distress, payment-network invisibility and automatic private-company markdowns overreach. Most company-specific causal claims remain unverified, and 2027 refinancing outcomes are genuinely unfinished.

Substack · 2026-05-27 ↗
Useful tension between household surveys and reported bank outcomes, with several independently verified premises. Neither survey dependence nor public-equity drawdowns alone establishes hidden bank losses or a universal private valuation decline. Guest positions, Eisman's probing questions and his explicit recap endorsements are kept separate.

How he reasons here

  • Separate household hardship from bank loan performance.
  • Distinguish payment status, expected-loss provisions and realized charge-offs.
  • Use consistent survey denominators and distinguish any use from dependence.
  • Trace private-credit funding, guarantees and retained exposure.
  • Compare private companies with public peers without assuming identical equity and enterprise-value changes.
  • Make maturities and sponsor incentives explicit.
  • Demand cohort evidence for immigration and affordability explanations.

Tools and charts discussed

Mentioned in the transcript; visual charts have not all been inspected.

  • Bank earnings calls and nonaccrual balances
  • CPI, PPI, energy inflation and real wages
  • BNPL usage and late-payment surveys
  • Warehouse lines and synthetic risk transfers
  • Software equity drawdowns and loan maturity ladders
  • Commercial-property debt maturities
  • Store-location demographic mapping
  • Receivables, invoice factoring and used-car auction observations
